translations.title: What Is Volume?
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will understand that solid objects have measurable attributes.
In previous grades, you learned that you can count the number of square tiles that cover a plane shape without gaps or overlaps to find the area of the shape. In this lesson, you explore the concept of volume as you build and compare objects made of cubes. You learn that objects can have different shapes but still take up the same amount of space and that we call this amount an object’s volume.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Explore volume by building objects with unit cubes and comparing them
- In previous grades, you learned that you can count the number of square tiles that cover a plane shape without gaps or overlaps to find the area of the shape
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Which one doesn’t belong? A Caption: A B Caption: B C Caption: C D Caption: D
Approach: “What do objects A, C, and D have in common?” (Each side or face of the shapes is a rectangle. You are all made from cubes of the same size.)
Example 2: Which is bigger? Explain or show your reasoning. A Caption: A B Caption: B Which is bigger? Explain or show your reasoning. A Caption: A B Caption: B What does it mean for an object to be “bigger”?
Approach: “How would you describe the amount of space each object takes up?” (It’s the same for both shapes. You are made from 8 individual cubes.) “Which object has greater volume?” (You are the same. You are both made from 8 cubes.)

translations.title: Measure Volume
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will understand that volume is the amount of unit cubes that fills a space.
You are introduced to rectangular prisms as you begin to informally use the structure of rectangular prisms to find the number of cubes in the prism. In previous grades, you learned to measure area by counting unit squares, decomposed a rectangular region into rows and columns, and multiplied the number of unit squares in a row by the number of rows or the number of unit squares in a column by the number of columns. Similarly, in this lesson, you make use of the layered structure in a rectangular prism to count the cubes in a more systematic way (MP7).
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Find the volume of solid figures, including rectangular prisms, in unit cubes, in a way that makes sense to them
- Understand that volume is measured in unit cubes
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

Example 1: Which one doesn’t belong? A Caption: A B Caption: B C Caption: C D Caption: D
Approach: “How many cubes are in object D? How did you count them?” (12, there are 6 on bottom and 6 on top) “What strategy would you use to count the cubes in the other objects?” (In object A, I can also see 2 groups of 6. In object B, I can see 2 groups of 6 minus 1. In object C, there is only one group of 6 and then there are 4 cubes and 2 cubes.)
Example 2: Partner A: Build an object using 8–12 cubes and give the object to Partner B. Partner B: Explain how you would count the number of cubes in the object. Learning goal: You will find the volume of a rectangular prism using its layered structure.
In previous lessons, you built objects, including rectangular prisms, with unit cubes and counted the number of cubes. In this lesson, you continue to count the number of unit cubes needed to build a rectangular prism, but now you are presented with images of prisms instead of the objects themselves. To encourage you to develop a systematic way to count the cubes, you are shown prisms made from larger numbers of cubes.

- In previous lessons, you built objects, including rectangular prisms, with unit cubes and counted the number of cubes

translations.title: Use Layers to Determine Volume PLC Activity
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will apply your understanding of the layered structure of rectangular prisms to find the volume of a prism when you cannot see all of the cubes.
In previous lessons, you used the layered structure to determine the volume of rectangular prisms that were filled with cubes. The purpose of this lesson is to extend your understanding of the structure of rectangular prisms by conceptualizing a base layer in a rectangular prism and utilizing it to find the volume in a fully- or partially-filled prism. You connect the layered structure to multiplication when you write and interpret expression that represent the volume of rectangular prisms (MP2, MP7).
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Describe and represent the volume of a rectangular prism as the product of the number of cubes in one layer and the number of layers
- Write and interpret expressions and equations in the context of the volume of rectangular prisms
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

translations.title: Side Lengths of Rectangular Prisms PLC Activity
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will formalize the language you use to describe the side lengths of a rectangular prism.
In previous lessons, you used the structure of a rectangular prism, namely layers, to find its volume. In this lesson, you describe the number of layers and the number of cubes in each layer in terms of the length, width, and height of the prism (MP6). You choose a base for the prism and recognize that the number of cubes in each layer is the product of the length and width of the chosen base.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Describe rectangular prisms in terms of your side lengths
- Find the volume of a right rectangular prism by multiplying the side lengths and connect that to finding volume by multiplying the area of the base by the height
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Here are 3 rectangular prisms. 1 Caption: 1 2 Caption: 2 3 Caption: 3 These rectangles represent bases of the prisms. A Caption: A B Caption: B C Caption: C Match each prism with a rectangle that represents its base. Note: Some prisms may match more than 1 rectangular base. Find the volume of each prism. Explain or show your reasoning.
Approach: “If prism 2 was resting on the 4 by 3 base, how many layers tall would the prism be?” (6 layers) “If prism 3 was resting on the 4 by 3 base, what would the height of the prism be?” (5 cubes)
Example 2: Here is a base of a rectangular prism. Fill out the table for the volumes of rectangular prisms with this base and different heights. height multiplication expression to represent the volume volume 1 2 3 10 25

translations.title: Expressions for Volume
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use your understanding of the structure of rectangular prisms to find volume and write numerical expressions to represent volume.
In a previous lesson you learned to find the volume of a rectangular prism by multiplying the number of cubes in a base layer by the number of layers. You connected this understanding to multiplication of length, width and height to find volume. You also used a two-dimensional representation of a base and its corresponding height to find the volume of a rectangular prism.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Find the volume of a right rectangular prism by multiplying the side lengths and connect that to finding volume by multiplying the area of the base by the height
- Write and interpret numerical expressions in the context of the volume of a rectangular prism
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Decide if each statement is true or false. Be prepared to explain your reasoning. \((4\times2)\times5=4\times(2\times5)\) \((2\times5)\times4=2\times20\) \(5\times4\times2=10\times40\)
Approach: Focus Question: “How can you justify your answer without evaluating both sides?” (I could see on the first equation that all of the factors are the same so it is true.)
Example 2: Match each rectangular prism with the expression(s) that represents its volume in cubic units. Be prepared to explain your reasoning. For each prism write one additional expression, not in the card sort, that represents its volume in cubic units.
Approach: \(6\times(5\times3)\) \((6\times5)\times3\) \(15\times6\) \((5\times3)\times6\) = \(15\times6\) “How does the equation relate to Prism A?” (Both expressions show that the prism has a height of 6. One expression shows the side lengths of the base. The other expression shows the area of the base.)

translations.title: Cubic Units of Measure
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will find the volume of rectangular prisms in cubic centimeters, cubic inches, and cubic feet.
In previous lessons, you used unit cubes with a side length of 1 unit to determine the volume of right rectangular prisms. In this lesson, the units are now a specific unit of measure. In grade 5, you use words, not exponents, when recording the cubic unit of measure, such as “cubic centimeters (cm),” “cubic feet (ft)” or “cubic inches (in).” The exponents in Grade 5 are limited to powers of 10, which will be addressed in a later unit.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Find the volume of rectangular prisms with standard units of measure by multiplying the base times the height or multiplying the length times the width times the height
- In previous lessons, you used unit cubes with a side length of 1 unit to determine the volume of right rectangular prisms
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: For each object, choose the cubic unit you would use to measure the volume: cubic centimeter, cubic inch, or cubic foot. object unit you would use the volume of a moving truck the volume of a freezer the volume of a juice box the volume of a classroom the volume of a dumpster the volume of a lunch box
Approach: “What if I only wrote 24 as the volume for the freezer? What questions would you have?” (I would wonder 24 what? If we don’t know the unit of measure, we don’t know how big the freezer actually is.) “What is the same about these measurements?” (You are all 24 units. You are all cubic units.)

translations.title: Figures Made of Prisms
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will recognize the structure of a solid figure made up of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms and understand that its volume is the sum of the volumes of the two rectangular prisms.
In previous lessons, you found the volume of right rectangular prisms represented in images where the cubes were shown or not shown. In this lesson, you build separate rectangular prisms and put them together to emphasize the relationship between the volume of the individual smaller prisms and the volume of the whole figure. Then you find volumes of figures made from two rectangular prisms without first building each part.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Explain that the volume of a figure composed of rectangular prisms is the sum of the volumes of the prisms
- Find the volume of a figure composed of rectangular prisms in which unit cubes are visible
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

Example 1: Which one doesn’t belong? A Caption: A B Caption: B C Caption: C D Caption: D
Approach: Identify the relevant attributes of the figure and use those attributes—not size or orientation—to justify the answer.
Example 2: Partner A, build a rectangular prism with 12 cubes. Partner B, build a rectangular prism with 10 cubes. Put your two rectangular prisms together to make one figure. What is the volume of the new figure? Explain or show your thinking. Diego and Jada put together two rectangular prisms to make this figure: Description: Two rectangular prisms, one attached...

How do you know?” (22 cubic units because I used 12 cubes and my partner used 10 cubes, so that’s 22 cubes altogether.) “What is the volume of the figure Diego and Jada made? How do you know?” (“30 cubic units. I broke it into two prisms and found your volumes and added them.”)

translations.title: All Kinds of Prisms
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will the mathematical purpose of this lesson is for you to apply what you have learned about finding the volumes of right rectangular prisms and figures composed of right rectangular prisms to solve real-world problems.
In previous lessons, you learned to find the volume of a right rectangular prism by multiplying the number of cubes in a layer by the number of layers. You found the volumes of rectangular prisms with and without the unit cubes showing. You used the associative property of multiplication to represent threefold whole-number products as volumes and learned to find the volume of rectangular prisms with whole-number side lengths by multiplying the length by the width by the height and multiplying the area of the base times the height.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving volume
- In previous lessons, you learned to find the volume of a right rectangular prism by multiplying the number of cubes in a layer by the number of layers
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

Approach: “What do Figures A, C, and D have in common?” (You all show individual cubes. You all have 5 as one of your side lengths.)
Example 2: For each problem, explain or show your reasoning. Han is filling a box with cubes. Below is a diagram of the box. How many cubes can fit in the box if Han completely packs it, without gaps between cubes? Clare bought a storage container for her art supplies. How are you different?” (You both got the same solution, but one person multiplied \(4\times9\) to get the area of the base and then multiplied the result by 5, but the other person chose to multiply \(4\times5\) first.) “How is the third problem different from the first two?” (It does not give us the length and width of the closet. Learning goal: You will use your understanding of volume of rectangular prisms to solve a real world problem.
This lesson is optional because it does not address any new mathematical content standards. This lesson does provide you with an opportunity to apply precursor skills of mathematical modeling. In previous lessons, you computed volumes.

- Find the volume of rectangular prisms with standard units of measure by multiplying the base times the height or multiplying the length times the width times the height
- This lesson is optional because it does not address any new mathematical content standards
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

translations.title: Share Sandwiches
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will relate equal shares of objects to division and to fractions.
In previous grades, you learned to interpret products of whole numbers, such as \(3 \times 5\) , as the total number of objects in 3 groups each containing 5 objects. You interpreted division, such as \(15 \div 3\) , to be either the number of groups when 15 things are put in groups of 3 or as the number of things in each group when 15 things are put in 3 equal groups. You also solve word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Interpret and represent contexts relating division and fractions in a way that makes sense to them
- In previous grades, you learned to interpret products of whole numbers, such as \(3 \times 5\) , as the total number of objects in 3 groups each containing 5 objects
- The addends are the quantities being combined and the sum is the resulting total; the expression must match the representation.

Approach: “Does each person get more than a full sandwich or less? How do you know?” (Less because there are more people than sandwiches or more because there are more sandwiches than people.) “This situation is about sharing. Step 1: Identify the quantities or expressions to compare.
Step 2: Represent or calculate each value accurately.
Step 3: Decide whether one is greater, less, or equal.
Step 4: Write or explain the comparison.
Step 5: Recheck both values before finalizing.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: deciding from appearance instead of actual values. Represent or calculate both quantities before comparing.
translations.quickSummary: You will relate equal shares of objects to division and to fractions. In previous grades, you learned to interpret products of whole numbers, such as \(3 \times 5\) , as the total number of objects in 3 groups each containing 5 objects.

translations.title: Share More Sandwiches
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will relate equal shares to division expressions and visual representations of fractions.
In the previous lesson, you explored the relationship between fractions and division by representing situations where some people shared some sandwiches. You used informal language to describe how you knew each person got about the same amount of sandwich. In this lesson, you recognize the relationship between a fraction and a division expression.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Represent the relationship between division and fractions with diagrams and expressions
- In the previous lesson, you explored the relationship between fractions and division by representing situations where some people shared some sandwiches
- The addends are the quantities being combined and the sum is the resulting total; the expression must match the representation.

Example 1: The large rectangle represents 1. What fraction of the large rectangle is shaded? Record an estimate that is: too low about right too high \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\) \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\) \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\)
Approach: “How did you make your about right estimate?” (It looks like there are about 5 of those shaded pieces in the whole rectangle so that’s about \(\frac{1}{5}\) .)
Example 2: Jada’s family made sandwiches to share at a family celebration. Complete the table to show how much sandwich each person gets. sandwiches being shared number of people sharing sandwiches amount of sandwich each person gets division expression 1 2 1 3 1 4 1 5 Choose one row from the table and represent your thinking with a diagram. translations.quickSummary: You will relate equal shares to division expressions and visual representations of fractions. In the previous lesson, you explored the relationship between fractions and division by representing situations where some people shared some sandwiches.

translations.title: Interpret Equations PLC Activity
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will write equations to represent division situations and relate each part of the equation to the situation.
In previous lessons, you developed the understanding that \(1 \div b = \frac{1}{b}\) . In this lesson, you deepen your understanding of the relationship between division and fractions.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Represent the relationship between division and fractions with equations
- In previous lessons, you developed the understanding that \(1 \div b = \frac{1}{b}\)
- Division can ask for the number of equal groups or the size of each group; interpret the quotient in the context.
translations.workedExamples:

translations.title: Division Situations
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will solve division problems when the quotient is a fraction or mixed number.
In previous lessons you solved equal sharing problems involving division of whole numbers with answers in the form of mixed numbers and fractions using diagrams. You noticed patterns and made generalizations about the relationship between the expression \(a \div b\) and the fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\) for specific values of \(a\) and \(b\) . You have observed that the numerator of the fraction is the number of objects being shared, while the denominator is the number of equal shares.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Solve problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions
- In previous lessons you solved equal sharing problems involving division of whole numbers with answers in the form of mixed numbers and fractions using diagrams
- Compare actual values or measured attributes, not the visual size or position of a drawing.

Example 1: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(35 \div 7\) \(1 \div 7\) \(36 \div 7\) \(37 \div 7\)
Approach: “What patterns do you notice?” (The solutions for \(35 \div 7\) , \(36 \div 7\) , \(37 \div 7\) increase by \(\frac {1}{7}\) ) “If we kept increasing the dividend by 1, what would be the next whole number quotient?” (6)

This story needs 4 objects and 6 equal shares.) “How did you use the diagram to help determine the number of objects and equal shares in your story?” (The number of objects is the number of wholes or large rectangles and the number...
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the whole.
Step 2: Partition or interpret the whole using equal parts.
Step 3: Count or name the relevant equal parts.
Step 4: Write or explain the fraction relationship.
Step 5: Check that the parts are equal and refer to the same whole.

translations.quickSummary: You will solve division problems when the quotient is a fraction or mixed number. In previous lessons you solved equal sharing problems involving division of whole numbers with answers in the form of mixed numbers and fractions using diagrams.

translations.title: Relate Division and Fractions
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will explain why \(a \div b = \frac{a}{b}\) and apply your understanding to flexibly interpret division situations and equations where the unknown is the numerator, denominator, or the value of the quotient.
In this lesson, you generalize your understanding that a fraction can be interpreted as division of the numerator by the denominator. You interpret situations where a certain amount of pounds of blueberries is shared with a certain number of people when the pounds of blueberries each person gets is equal to 1, greater than 1, and less than 1. Then, you construct arguments about why an equation would make sense for any numerator and for any denominator.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Explain the relationship between division and fractions
- In this lesson, you generalize your understanding that a fraction can be interpreted as division of the numerator by the denominator
- Compare actual values or measured attributes, not the visual size or position of a drawing.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Decide if each statement is true or false. Be prepared to explain your reasoning. \(5 \div 2 = \frac{5}{2}\) \(\frac{5}{2} = 5\frac{1}{2}\) \(\frac{6}{2} = 3\)
Approach: \(5\frac{1}{2}\) \(\frac{5}{2}\) “How are these expressions the same? How are you different?” (You both have 5 and 2 in them. You both show halves. \(5\frac{1}{2}\) means 5 wholes plus one half and \(\frac{5}{2}\) means 5 groups of one half.)
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the total and the required number or size of groups.
Step 2: Represent the sharing or grouping.
Step 3: Write the division relationship.
Step 4: Find the quotient using an efficient method.
Step 5: Check by multiplying the quotient and divisor when appropriate.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: confusing the number of groups with the size of each group. Check what the quotient means in the context.
translations.quickSummary: You will explain why \(a \div b = \frac{a}{b}\) and apply your understanding to flexibly interpret division situations and equations where the unknown is the numerator, denominator, or the value of the quotient. In this lesson, you generalize your understanding that a fraction can be interpreted as division of the numerator by the denominator.

translations.title: Relate Division and Multiplication
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will understand that dividing an amount into a whole number of equal parts can be interpreted as multiplying the same amount by a unit fraction.
In previous lessons, you interpreted a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator, and equivalently, as a whole number divided into equal sized pieces. In this lesson, you relate division of two whole numbers to multiplying a whole number by a unit fraction. In the first activity, you are given an opportunity to solve a division problem using any strategy and, in the synthesis, you examine how the solution can be interpreted in terms of multiplication or division.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Explore the relationship between multiplication and division
- In previous lessons, you interpreted a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator, and equivalently, as a whole number divided into equal sized pieces
- Measurement units must be equal in size and placed or interpreted without gaps, overlaps, or a shifted starting point.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(3 \times \frac{1}{2}\) \(3 \times \frac{2}{2}\) \(3 \times \frac{3}{2}\) \(5 \times \frac{3}{2}\)
Approach: “How do we know this is true?” (You are both equal to \(15 \div 2\) or 7 is \(\frac{14}{2}\) so \(7 \frac{1}{2}\) is \(\frac{15}{2}\) ).
Example 2: Lin and Han ran a 3 mile relay race as a team. They each ran the same distance. Draw a diagram to represent the situation. Take turns describing to your partner how your diagrams represent the situation. How far did each person run?
Approach: “How does each of these expressions represent the situation?” (3 miles was divided into 2 equal parts, each person ran \(1\frac{1}{2}\) miles or \(\frac{3}{2}\) miles which can be thought of as \(3\times \frac{1}{2}\) .
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify what needs to be measured.
Step 2: Choose the required unit and correct starting point.
Step 3: Place or interpret equal-size units accurately.
Step 4: Count or calculate the units and record the measure.
Step 5: Check the endpoint, scale, and unit label.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: using unequal units, leaving gaps, overlapping units, or starting at the wrong point. Check the unit and endpoints.
translations.quickSummary: You will understand that dividing an amount into a whole number of equal parts can be interpreted as multiplying the same amount by a unit fraction. In previous lessons, you interpreted a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator, and equivalently, as a whole number divided into equal sized pieces.

translations.title: Divide to Multiply Unit Fractions PLC Activity
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will solve problems involving multiplication of whole numbers by unit fractions and represent the problems with equations and diagrams.
In this lesson you interpret situations and solve problems that involve products of a whole number and a fraction. You solve story problems in a way that makes sense to them and match stories with diagrams and expressions. You work with expressions and flexibly interpret a diagram to extend your understanding of the relationship between fractions and multiplication and division.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Connect division to multiplication of a whole number by a unit fraction
- In this lesson you interpret situations and solve problems that involve products of a whole number and a fraction
- Measurement units must be equal in size and placed or interpreted without gaps, overlaps, or a shifted starting point.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: What number is marked on the number line? Record an estimate that is: too low about right too high \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\) \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\) \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\)
Approach: “Is the number that goes in the box more or less than half of 5? How do you know?” (Less, since it is less than half the way to 5.) “How does this help you estimate the value?” (I know half of 5 is \(2 \frac{1}{2}\) , so it is less than that.)
Example 2: Solve each problem. Draw a diagram if it is helpful. Mai ran \(\frac{1}{4}\) the length of her road, which is 9 miles long. How far did Mai run? Han ran \(\frac{1}{4}\) the length of his road, which is 7 miles long. How far did Han run?
Approach: “What are some expressions that represent the distance Han ran?” ( \(7 \div 4\) , \(1 \frac{3}{4}\) , \(\frac{7}{4}\) , \(\frac{1}{4}\times7\) ) “How does each of these expressions represent the distance Han ran?” (He ran \(\frac{1}{4}\) of 7 miles and we can write that as \(\frac{1}{4} \times 7\) . Step 5: Check the endpoint, scale, and unit label.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: using unequal units, leaving gaps, overlapping units, or starting at the wrong point. Check the unit and endpoints.
translations.quickSummary: You will solve problems involving multiplication of whole numbers by unit fractions and represent the problems with equations and diagrams. In this lesson you interpret situations and solve problems that involve products of a whole number and a fraction.

translations.title: Divide to Multiply Non-unit Fractions
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will represent and solve problems involving a non-unit fraction.
In this lesson, you to make sense of the product of a whole number and a non-unit fraction. You relate the product of a whole number and a non-unit fraction to the product of a whole number and a unit fraction. You will have more opportunities to multiply a whole number by a fraction in the next section, systematically using the idea of area.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Connect division to multiplication of a whole number by a non-unit fraction
- In this lesson, you to make sense of the product of a whole number and a non-unit fraction
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

Example 1: Decide if each statement is true or false. Approach: “How can you explain why \(\frac{2}{3} \times 6 = 2 \times (\frac{1}{4} \times6)\) is false without finding the value of both sides?” (It can't be true because \(\frac{2}{3} \times 6=2\times\frac{1}{3}\times6\) .)
Example 2: Find the value of each expression. Explain or show your reasoning. Draw a diagram if it is helpful. \(\frac{1}{5} \times 3\) \(\frac{2}{5} \times 3\) \(\frac{3}{5} \times 3\)

There is 1 and then 2 and then 3.) “How can you use the value of \(\frac{1}{5} \times 3\) to help find the value of \(\frac{2}{5} \times 3\) ?” (I can just double the result because it’s \(\frac{2}{5}\) instead of \(\frac{1}{5}\) .) “What...

translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: using unequal units, leaving gaps, overlapping units, or starting at the wrong point. Check the unit and endpoints.
translations.quickSummary: You will represent and solve problems involving a non-unit fraction. In this lesson, you to make sense of the product of a whole number and a non-unit fraction.

translations.title: Relate Area to Multiplication
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will calculate the area of a rectangle whose side lengths are a unit fraction and a whole number in a way that makes sense to them.
You build on your understanding of multiplication and area from grade 3 as you work with areas with fractional side lengths. The commutative property allows you to find products in a way that makes sense to them. For example a student might find the area of a rectangle with side lengths \(\frac{1}{2}\) and 4 by thinking of 4 groups of \(\frac{1}{2}\) .

- Find the area of a rectangle with a unit fraction side length in a way that makes sense to them

translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will find the area of rectangles with one non-unit fractional side length and one whole number side length.

In this lesson, you will find the area of rectangles with a whole number side length and a non-unit fraction side length. You will apply what you learned in earlier lessons to area representations and recognize that a side length of \(\frac{a}{b}\) is equivalent to a side length of \(a \times \frac{1}{b}\) .

translations.title: Fractional Side Lengths Greater Than 1 PLC Activity
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will find the area of a rectangle where one of the side lengths is a fraction greater than 1.
In previous lessons, you multiplied fractions by whole numbers and found the area of rectangles with one fractional side length when the fraction was less than 1. You used visual representations to support your reasoning. For example, you use this picture to explain why \(\frac{2}{3} \times 4 = (2 \times 4) \times \frac{1}{3}\) .
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Find the area of a rectangle with one fractional side length greater than 1 in a way that makes sense to them
- Represent the area of a rectangle with a multiplication expression
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

Example 1: Decide if each statement is true or false. Be prepared to explain your reasoning. \(10 \div 3 = 10 \times \frac{1}{3}\) \(10 \div 3 = 10 \frac{1}{3}\) \(\frac{10}{3} = 5 \times \frac{2}{3}\)

translations.title: Divide Unit Fractions by Whole Numbers

- Measurement units must be equal in size and placed or interpreted without gaps, overlaps, or a shifted starting point.
translations.workedExamples:

Approach: “How did you find the value of \(3 \div \frac{1}{10}\) ?” (I know that there are ten \(\frac{1}{10}\) s in 1 so there are thirty \(\frac{1}{10}\) s in 3.)

Step 2: Partition or interpret the whole using equal parts.
Step 3: Count or name the relevant equal parts.
Step 4: Write or explain the fraction relationship.
Step 5: Check that the parts are equal and refer to the same whole.

translations.quickSummary: You will apply your understanding of fraction multiplication and division to solve problems in context. In previous lessons, you multiplied fractions and divided whole numbers and unit fractions.

translations.title: Fraction Games
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use your understanding of fractions and division to make the largest and smallest expressions using given numbers.
You work together with expressions involving a unit fraction divided by a whole number and a whole number divided by a unit fraction. In both activities, you write multiplication and division expressions, given specific digits to choose from. In Activity 1, you are applying what you learned to strategically write expressions that represent the greatest product or quotient.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Multiply and divide with fractions
- You work together with expressions involving a unit fraction divided by a whole number and a whole number divided by a unit fraction
- Measurement units must be equal in size and placed or interpreted without gaps, overlaps, or a shifted starting point.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: \(28 \times 2 \frac{8}{9}\) Record an estimate that is: too low about right too high \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\) \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\) \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\)
Approach: “How does \(28 \times 2\frac{8}{9}\) compare to \(28 \times 2\) ? How do you know?” (It’s larger because \(2 \frac{8}{9}\) is greater than 2.) “Why is \(28 \times 3\) a good estimate?” (Because \(2\frac{8}{9}\) is really close to 3.) “Is \(28 \times 2\frac{8}{9}\) greater or less than \(28 \times 3\) ? How do you know?” (Less because \(2\frac{8}{9}\) is less than 3.)
Example 2: For each expression, work with your partner to decide what is the greatest product or quotient you can make with the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. For each expression, you can only use each number once. Explain or show your reasoning....
Approach: “Why is \(6 \div \frac{1}{5}\) a good choice for making this expression as large as possible?” (When I find the value I am multiplying 6 and 5. Those are the two biggest numbers so I know that will give me the biggest value.) “Is there another choice for filling in the blanks that gives the same value?” (Yes, I can also do \(5 \div \frac{1}{6}\) .)

translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: naming parts as fractions when the parts are not equal. Check that the whole is partitioned into equal parts.
translations.quickSummary: You will use your understanding of fractions and division to make the largest and smallest expressions using given numbers. You work together with expressions involving a unit fraction divided by a whole number and a whole number divided by a unit fraction.

translations.title: How Much in the Group? (optional)
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will solve fraction division problems that ask: “How many in one group?”.
In this optional lesson, you solve problems where a whole number quantity is a unit fraction of an unknown whole number. In these situations you may rely on your understanding of the relationship between multiplication and division. For example, if 8 ounces is \(\frac{1}{4}\) of the amount of water in a bottle, you might represent this with a tape diagram: The tape diagram suggests the equation \(8 = \frac{1}{4} \times {?}\) which you will likely solve by seeing that \({?} = 4 \times 8\) .
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Represent and solve problems involving division of a whole number by a unit fraction
- In this optional lesson, you solve problems where a whole number quantity is a unit fraction of an unknown whole number
- Measurement units must be equal in size and placed or interpreted without gaps, overlaps, or a shifted starting point.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: What number goes in the blank? Record an estimate that is: too low about right too high \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\) \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\) \(\phantom{\hspace{2.5cm} \\ \hspace{2.5cm}}\)
Approach: “What strategies did you use to determine the number that goes in the blank?” (I tried to see how many 15's fit in the whole rectangle.)
Example 2: If \(\frac {1}{3}\) of the class is 9 students, how many students are in the class? Explain or show your reasoning. Explain how each of these equations represents this situation. \(\frac {1}{3} \times \underline{\hspace{1 cm}} = 9\) \(\underline{\hspace{1 cm}} \div 3 = 9\) \(3 \times 9 = \underline{\hspace{1 cm}}\)
Approach: \(27 \div 3 = 9\) \(3 \times 9 = 27\) “What is the relationship between these two equations? Discuss with a partner.” (You are like opposites. 27 divided into 3 equal groups is 9 and 3 groups of 9 is 27.) \(\frac {1}{3} \times 27 = 9\) “How does this equation represent the situation?” (We know that \(\frac {1}{3}\) of the class is 9, so the class must have 27 kids in it, because \(\frac {1}{3}\) of 27 is 9.)

Step 2: Partition or interpret the whole using equal parts.
Step 3: Count or name the relevant equal parts.
Step 4: Write or explain the fraction relationship.
Step 5: Check that the parts are equal and refer to the same whole.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: naming parts as fractions when the parts are not equal. Check that the whole is partitioned into equal parts.
translations.quickSummary: You will solve fraction division problems that ask: “How many in one group?”. In this optional lesson, you solve problems where a whole number quantity is a unit fraction of an unknown whole number.

translations.title: Estimate and Find Products
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will make estimates and calculations of products.
In grade 4, you multiplied two-digit by two-digit and one-digit by up to four-digit numbers using strategies based on place value understanding and the properties of operations. You learned a partial product strategy for multiplication and represented it with diagrams and equations. Expect to see a wide range of strategies from you and be sure to listen to them as you explain your reasoning.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Multiply multi-digit numbers in a way that makes sense to them
- In grade 4, you multiplied two-digit by two-digit and one-digit by up to four-digit numbers using strategies based on place value understanding and the properties of operations
- Multiplication can represent equal groups, arrays, rates, or scaling; each factor must have a clear meaning in the context.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find the value of each product mentally. \(50 \times 6\) \(50 \times 60\) \(50 \times 600\) \(600 \times 500\)
Approach: “How can we use \(5 \times 6\) to find the value of each product?” ( \(50 \times 6 = 5 \times 6 \times 10\) , \(50 \times 60 = 5 \times 6 \times 10 \times 10\) , \(50 \times 600 = 5 \times 6 \times 10 \times 100\) , \(600 \times 500 = 6 \times 5 \times 100 \times 100\) ) “Why does each product in the number talk have one more 0 in it than the previous product?” (Because one of the factors has an additional 0.)
Example 2: Which estimate for the product \(18 \times 149\) is most reasonable? Explain or show your reasoning. \(2,\!000\) \(4,\!000\) \(3,\!000\) \(1,\!500\) Are any of the estimates unreasonable? Explain or show your reasoning. Do you think the actual product will be more or less than your estimate? Explain or show your reasoning.
Approach: “Why do you think \(3,\!000\) is a good estimate?” (18 is close to 20 and 149 is very close to 150 and I know \(20 \times 150 = 3,\!000\) .) “Is the value of \(18 \times 149\) greater than or less than \(3,\!000\) ? How do you know?” (Less, because 18 is less than 20 and 149 is less than 150.) “Can you estimate how much less?” (About 300, because I added 2 to 18 to get 20 and \(2 \times 149\) is about 300.)
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify what the task asks you to find or show.
Step 2: Represent the important quantities or relationships.
Step 3: Apply the key idea from the lesson.
Step 4: Explain how the representation supports the result.
Step 5: Check that the result matches the question.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: jumping to an answer before checking that the representation matches the quantities and relationship in the task.
translations.quickSummary: You will make estimates and calculations of products. In grade 4, you multiplied two-digit by two-digit and one-digit by up to four-digit numbers using strategies based on place value understanding and the properties of operations.

translations.title: Partial Products in Diagrams
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will multiply multi-digit whole numbers using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations.
This lesson builds on the partial products representation you saw in grade 4 to help organize calculations of whole number products. This becomes even more important for the product of a two-digit and three-digit number as the number of partial products is larger, depending on the diagram that is used.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Interpret partial products diagrams
- Multiply a three-digit number and a two-digit number
- The addends are the quantities being combined and the sum is the resulting total; the expression must match the representation.

translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the equal groups, rate, or scaling relationship.
Step 2: Represent the groups or factors.
Step 3: Write the multiplication relationship.
Step 4: Calculate the product using an efficient method.

translations.quickSummary: You will multiply multi-digit whole numbers using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. This lesson builds on the partial products representation you saw in grade 4 to help organize calculations of whole number products.

translations.title: Partial Products in Algorithms
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will multiply multi-digit whole numbers using partial products.
In previous lessons, you multiplied three-digit numbers and two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. In this lesson, you move from diagrams to an algorithm that records partial products which you used in an earlier course when multiplying a two-digit number and a two-digit number.

- Multiply a three-digit number and a two-digit number
- Represent a partial products algorithm
- Multiplication can represent equal groups, arrays, rates, or scaling; each factor must have a clear meaning in the context.

translations.title: Standard Algorithm: One-digit and Multi-digit Numbers with Composing
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use the standard algorithm to multiply up to five-digit numbers and one-digit numbers.

In this lesson, you extend your understanding of the standard algorithm to multiply up to five-digit numbers and one-digit numbers, including problems where one or more new units are composed. This is the first in a series of lessons to support you in developing fluency using the standard algorithm to multiply multi-digit numbers. - Representation

translations.title: Standard Algorithm: Multi-digit Numbers without Composing
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use the standard algorithm to multiply up to three-digit numbers and two-digit numbers without composing a new unit.
In a previous lesson, you used the standard algorithm to multiply up to five-digit numbers by one-digit numbers. You connected the standard algorithm to a different algorithm that uses partial products. In this lesson, you find products of a three-digit number and a two-digit number when composing is not required.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Use the standard algorithm to multiply up to three-digit numbers and two-digit numbers, without composing new units
- In a previous lesson, you used the standard algorithm to multiply up to five-digit numbers by one-digit numbers
- Measurement units must be equal in size and placed or interpreted without gaps, overlaps, or a shifted starting point.

Example 1: Find the value of each product mentally. \(20 \times 3\) \(24 \times 3\) \(120 \times 3\) \(140 \times 3\)

Example 2: Two algorithms for finding the value of \(413 \times 21\) are shown. Description: multiply. four hundred thirteen times 21. 9 rows. First row: four hundred thirteen. translations.explanation:

Key ideas:

- In previous lessons you have used the standard algorithm to find products of 3-digit and 2-digit numbers including products with newly composed units

translations.title: Multiplication Fluency
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will play games to continue to develop fluency with multiplying multi-digit numbers with the standard algorithm.
In this lesson, you continue to find products of a 2-digit number and a 3-digit number with a strategic goal. You continue to play Greatest Product and you also use 5 given digits to try to make a product that is as close as possible to a given number. This is more challenging than making the greatest product as rather than putting the largest digits in the largest place values you will need to experiment or reflect about how each digit in the numbers influences the value of the product.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Solve problems that involve the multiplication of multi-digit numbers
- In this lesson, you continue to find products of a 2-digit number and a 3-digit number with a strategic goal
- The addends are the quantities being combined and the sum is the resulting total; the expression must match the representation.

translations.title: The Birds

translations.keyConceptsAndRules:

One way to find a difference, such as \(135 - 28\) , is to add on, first 2, then 5, then 100, finding that the difference is 107.

translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will represent situations by plotting and interpreting points on the coordinate grid.

In this lesson, you practice using the standard algorithm when one or more of the factors includes several zeros. The zeros are at the end of the number so you may identify each zero as representing a factor of 10 and work with smaller numbers to find the product.

- Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm

Approach: “Why is \(10,\!000 \times 900\) a good estimate for the product?” (10,000 is just 1 more than 9,999 and 896 is close to 900.) “What is the value of \(10,\!000 \times 900\) ? How do you know?” (9,000,000 because the two numbers have 6 factors of 10 combined.)
Example 2: Find the value of the product. Below is Kiran’s work finding the value of the product \(650 \times 27\) . Is his answer reasonable? Explain your reasoning. Approach: “Why doesn’t 5,850 make sense?” ( \(650 \times 10 = 6,\!500 \) so \(650 \times 27\) should be a lot larger than 6,500.) “What makes sense about Kiran’s work?” ( \(650 \times 2 =1,\!300\) , but he needs to multiply \(650\times2\times10\) .) “How do we know that 17,550 is a reasonable value for the product?” (Because \(600 \times 30 =18,\!000\) .)

In this lesson, you reason about how the factors in a problem can influence the multiplication strategy you use. You recognize that the standard algorithm can be more useful in some cases than others.

Step 3: Write an addition relationship that matches the representation.
Step 4: Find the total using an efficient strategy.
Step 5: Check that the total matches the original quantities.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: counting an item twice or combining the wrong quantities. Check the addends and verify the total.
translations.quickSummary: You will practice adding fractions with unlike denominators. In previous units, you learned how to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators.

translations.title: What’s the Difference?
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will practice subtracting fractions with unlike denominators.
This lesson complements the previous lesson except that you are looking to make the greatest or smallest differences rather than sums. Trying to make the greatest difference supports strategies like you used in the previous lesson, looking to choose a large numerator and small denominator for one fraction and a small numerator and large denominator for the other (MP7). Trying to make a small difference brings a new feature into play, namely that the difference can be 0 if the fractions are equivalent.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Subtract fractions and mixed numbers
- This lesson complements the previous lesson except that you are looking to make the greatest or smallest differences rather than sums
- Subtraction can represent taking away, comparing quantities, or finding a missing addend; the representation must match the situation.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find the value of each difference mentally. \(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{6}\) \(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\) \(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{4}{6}\) \(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{4}\)
Approach: “How are the differences related?” ( \(\frac{1}{6}\) and \(\frac{1}{2}\) are \(\frac{2}{3}\) so I can take away \(\frac{1}{6}\) and that gives me \(\frac{1}{2}\) or I can take away \(\frac{1}{2}\) and that gives me \(\frac{1}{6}\) .)
Example 2: Use the directions to play Greatest Difference with a partner. Spin the spinner. Each player writes the number that was spun in an empty box for Round 1. Be sure your partner cannot see your paper. Once a number is written down, it cannot be changed. Continue spinning and writing numbers in the empty boxes until all 4 boxes have been filled. Find the...
Approach: “What is the biggest difference possible between fractions in this game? How do you know?” ( \(\frac{6}{1} - \frac{1}{6}\) since \(\frac{6}{1}\) is the biggest number and \(\frac{1}{6}\) is the smallest.) “Did anyone get \(\frac{6}{1} - \frac{1}{6}\) as one of your fractions?” (Answers vary.)
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the whole and the part being removed or compared.
Step 2: Represent the situation with objects, a drawing, number line, or equation.
Step 3: Write a subtraction relationship that matches the representation.
Step 4: Find the difference using an efficient strategy.
Step 5: Check the result with the original quantities or a related addition fact.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: mixing up the whole and the part being removed or compared. Check that the subtraction relationship matches the representation.
translations.quickSummary: You will practice subtracting fractions with unlike denominators. This lesson complements the previous lesson except that you are looking to make the greatest or smallest differences rather than sums.

translations.title: Decimal Game Day
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will practice adding and subtracting decimals.
In a previous unit, you learned how to add and subtract decimals. In this lesson, you play games where you practice adding and subtracting decimals. The first game resembles the games you played in the previous two lessons.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths
- In a previous unit, you learned how to add and subtract decimals
- Measurement units must be equal in size and placed or interpreted without gaps, overlaps, or a shifted starting point.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Decide if each statement true or false. Be prepared to explain your reasoning. \(0.99 + 0.1 = 0.9 + 0.1 + 0.09\) \(0.99 + 0.01 = 0.9 + 0.1\) \(0.99 + 0.1 = 1.99\)
Approach: “How can you justify your answer without evaluating both sides?” (For the first problem, I noticed that there are 9 tenths on the right and left and also 10 hundredths. For the third problem, I saw that the right hand side is almost 2 so it's much larger than the left hand side.)
Example 2: Use the directions to play Race to One or One Tenth with your partner. If there is time, play both versions of the game. Race to One Roll the number cube. Decide if you want the number to represent tenths or hundredths. Add the number to the last sum on your score sheet. If it is your first turn, you will add the number you roll to zero. Take turns...
Approach: “How are the games different?” (In Race to One, I am aiming for 1 and in Race to One Tenth I am trying to get 0.1. When I get close to 1 in Race to One I have to choose hundredths and when I get close to 0.1 in Race to One Tenth I have to choose thousandths.)
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify what the task asks you to find or show.
Step 2: Represent the important quantities or relationships.
Step 3: Apply the key idea from the lesson.
Step 4: Explain how the representation supports the result.
Step 5: Check that the result matches the question.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: jumping to an answer before checking that the representation matches the quantities and relationship in the task.
translations.quickSummary: You will practice adding and subtracting decimals. In a previous unit, you learned how to add and subtract decimals.

translations.title: Multiply Fractions Game Day PLC Activity
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will practice multiplying fractions.
In previous lessons, you learned how to multiply fractions by whole numbers and fractions. In this lesson, you practice multiplying fractions. You spin numbers and use them as the numerators and denominators of two fractions.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction
- In previous lessons, you learned how to multiply fractions by whole numbers and fractions
- Multiplication can represent equal groups, arrays, rates, or scaling; each factor must have a clear meaning in the context.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(\frac{1}{3}\times3\) \(\frac{1}{3}\times4\) \(\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{6}{3}\) \(\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{1}{4}\)
Approach: “How did you find this product?” (I took the products of the numerators and denominators. I knew \(\frac{6}{3}\) is 2, so it’s \(\frac{2}{3}\) .)
Example 2: Use the directions to play Fraction Multiplication Compare with your partner. Spin the spinner. Write the number you spun in one of the empty blank boxes. Once you write a number, you cannot change it. Player two spins and writes the number on their game board. Continue taking turns until all four blank boxes are filled. Multiply your fractions. The...
Approach: “Which numbers were easiest to choose where to put on the game board? Why?” (When I got an 8 or 9 I knew to put it in the numerator to make a bigger fraction. When I got a 1 or 2 I knew to put it in the denominator to get the biggest possible fraction.) “Which numbers were hardest to choose where to put on the game board? Why?” (The middle numbers like 4, 5, and 6. I did not want them in the denominator because...
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the equal groups, rate, or scaling relationship.
Step 2: Represent the groups or factors.
Step 3: Write the multiplication relationship.
Step 4: Calculate the product using an efficient method.
Step 5: Check the product against the representation or context.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: treating unequal groups as equal groups. Check what each factor represents before multiplying.
translations.quickSummary: You will practice multiplying fractions. In previous lessons, you learned how to multiply fractions by whole numbers and fractions.

translations.title: Notice and Wonder
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will apply your understanding of fractions as division to create a Notice and Wonder activity.
After the warm-up, you create your own Notice and Wonder activity and then facilitate your Notice and Wonder with other you in the class.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator
- After the warm-up, you create your own Notice and Wonder activity and then facilitate your Notice and Wonder with other you in the class
- Division can ask for the number of equal groups or the size of each group; interpret the quotient in the context.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find an image that would encourage your classmates to notice and wonder about sharing and interpreting the result as a fraction. Fill in the possible things students might notice and wonder about your image. Students may notice: Students may wonder:
Approach: “What questions do you still have about creating a Notice and Wonder?” (How do I know what someone will notice or wonder? What if you don't think of division when you see the picture? What if you focus on a part of the picture I was not thinking about?)
Example 2: Find an image that you find interesting and would encourage your classmates to notice and wonder about a mathematical topic you have learned this year. Fill in the possible things students might notice and wonder about your image. Students may notice: Students may wonder:
Approach: Identify the total and how it is being shared or grouped, represent the groups, divide, and check the quotient.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the total and the required number or size of groups.
Step 2: Represent the sharing or grouping.
Step 3: Write the division relationship.
Step 4: Find the quotient using an efficient method.
Step 5: Check by multiplying the quotient and divisor when appropriate.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: confusing the number of groups with the size of each group. Check what the quotient means in the context.
translations.quickSummary: You will apply your understanding of fractions as division to create a Notice and Wonder activity. After the warm-up, you create your own Notice and Wonder activity and then facilitate your Notice and Wonder with other you in the class.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers with unlike denominators
- After the warm-up, three activities are given, but it is not expected that you do all three
- Choose a representation that matches the quantities and relationship, then use it to justify and check the result.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Decide if each statement is true or false. Be prepared to explain your reasoning. \(\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{8} = \frac{3}{8}+\frac{3}{8}\) \(\frac{7}{5}+\frac{2}{3} = \frac{21}{15}+\frac{8}{15}\) \(\frac{8}{9}+\frac{5}{12}=\frac{32}{36}+\frac{15}{36}\)
Approach: “What did the writer of this activity have to pay attention to when you designed this activity?” (Some equations are true and some are false. Some terms on both sides are equal. Approach: Represent the quantities or relationships clearly, apply the lesson idea, and check that the result answers the question.

translations.title: Which One Doesn’t Belong?
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will apply your understanding of volume to create a Which One Doesn’t Belong activity.
After the warm-up, three activities are given, but it is not expected that you do all three. As the activities progress, there is one additional element missing from the Which One Doesn’t Belong.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Categorize shapes by your shared attributes
- After the warm-up, three activities are given, but it is not expected that you do all three
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Which one doesn’t belong? A Caption: A B Description: 6-sided rectangular prism. Straight sides. All side lengths meet at right angles. Side lengths. Bottom, 7 units. Left side rises 1 unit, then goes right 2 units, goes up 1 unit, then goes right 5 units, then goes down 2 units. Width shown as 3 units. Caption: B C Caption: C D Caption: D
Approach: “What did the writer of this activity have to pay attention to when you designed this activity?” (the number of sides, the types of angles or corners, the way you were oriented, how many shapes there were in each)
Example 2: Choose 3 shapes from the set of cards. Draw a fourth shape to complete the Which One Doesn’t Belong. For each shape, discuss one reason why it does not belong. Which one doesn’t belong? A B C D
Approach: Identify the relevant attributes of the figure and use those attributes—not size or orientation—to justify the answer.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the figure and the attributes named in the task.
Step 2: Measure, count, or compare sides, angles, corners, or other relevant features.
Step 3: Use the attributes to classify, construct, or reason about the figure.
Step 4: Explain which attributes support the result.
Step 5: Check that the conclusion does not depend only on size or orientation.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: classifying a figure by appearance, size, or orientation. Use its mathematical attributes instead.
translations.quickSummary: You will apply your understanding of volume to create a Which One Doesn’t Belong activity. After the warm-up, three activities are given, but it is not expected that you do all three.
